title: Ikkyu
hookLine: the wild Zen poet-monk who mocked pomp

cards: A Zen monk walks through town in shabby robes, and people say he drinks in taverns and writes poems that would make an abbot blush. He calls himself Crazy Cloud.
Stories say that when his teacher offered him the certificate that proves a student's awakening, he wouldn't keep it.
Another has him at New Year, while everyone celebrates, carrying a skull on a stick through the streets as a reminder. Not all these tales can be checked. But they all point the same way.

teach.b: Ikkyu was a Japanese Rinzai Zen monk and poet, remembered more through his poems, gathered in what's known in English as the Crazy Cloud Anthology, than through any sermon. First, what he aimed at.
His poems jab at monks who wear fine robes, collect titles, sell certificates of awakening and run temples like businesses. For him, all that ceremony could become a costume over an empty room.
Zen was supposed to strip things down to the plain truth, and here it was dressing up.
Second, how he aimed: not with a treatise, but with laughter, scandal and verse. His poems talk openly about wine, love and the body, things a respectable monk was supposed to keep quiet about.

Readers argue about how literally to take them. Some hear a monk refusing to pretend he's purer than he is. Others hear a teacher using shock the way a Zen master uses a shout, to knock a student loose.

Third, the twist. Tradition says that late in life Ikkyu was asked to lead Daitokuji, the kind of temple he'd mocked, and he took up the work of rebuilding it. The wild monk didn't drop out of the tradition.

teach.h: HE LOVED IT ENOUGH TO LAUGH.
teach.b: He loved it enough to laugh at it. And that closes the week: Eisai's tea, the old cook in the sun, Dogen's just sitting, forgetting the self and being-time, Nichiren's chant, and now Ikkyu's laugh.
Each is its own path, but side by side they share a small thread: meet what's here, without the extras.

how: Ikkyu is remembered in Japan through his poems, his calligraphy and folk stories, and Zen students and teachers read his verse as a reminder not to confuse the robes and ranks of practice with practice itself.

games.q: your teacher offers you the certificate that proves your awakening. you're Ikkyu. what do you do?
o: frame it and hang it in the hall
games.why: stories say Ikkyu wouldn't keep it: a piece of paper was exactly the kind of pomp he mocked.

practice: Sit easily and bring to mind one small way you dress yourself up: a title you like to mention, an opinion you defend a bit too loudly, the version of yourself you post.

Look at it kindly, the way Ikkyu might from a tavern doorway, and let a smile come if it wants to. You don't have to throw it away; just see the costume as a costume, and rest in whatever is under it.

wordCard.voice: Ikkyu. The Japanese Zen poet-monk who called himself Crazy Cloud and used laughter and verse to puncture pomp. Today's word.
